---
title: "One Flowchart, So Every Table Looks Like It Came from the Same Designer"
author: Hrudith Lakshminarasimman
date: 2026-08-11
---

Ask an AI coding agent to turn a CSV into a [**Great Tables**][great-tables] display
table with no guidance at all, and you will get *something*, but not the same
something twice. One run colors the revenue column, the next colors margin, the one
after that colors both. One run adds a heading band, the next does not. Sometimes the
agent forgets a subtitle, or a source note, or leaves an obvious row label sitting in
the body instead of the stub. Ask the same question ten times and you can get ten
tables that do not look like they came from the same product.

### Why does that happen?

A general-purpose model's sense of what makes a table look good is not stable from one
run to the next, even against the exact same input. Left alone, it re-derives taste
every time it is asked, and taste re-derived from scratch on every run is, almost by
definition, inconsistent. So we did not try to make the model better at inventing
table design. We tried to stop asking it to invent one at all, and instead gave it an
[**Agent Skill**][great-docs-skills]: a folder of instructions and reference files
that the agent is required to read before it writes any code, so the decisions that
used to be a fresh judgment call on every run become a fixed, repeatable branch
instead.

### One flowchart, not a menu

The skill is written as a flowchart, not a menu of options. For every part of a table
there is one deterministic rule, or one explicit branch keyed off what the data
looks like, so the same input always produces the same output:

```
1. UNDERSTAND THE DATA   grain? identifiers? measures? categories? units? quality?
                         clean -> ONE correctly-typed DataFrame
                         validate request vs data (blank table if unanswerable)
2. ORGANIZE COLUMNS      show/hide, limit rows, stub (default), groups (gated),
                         spanners (column groups), name the hero column
3. BIG COLOR             at most 2 colored MEASURES (the hero if only 1); encoding
                         by data shape, gradients use sequential/diverging,
                         everything else uses a fixed solid palette
4. HEADING BAND          any Big Color? light band. none? dark saturated band
5. SMALL COLOR           fixed checklist: borders, dividers, striping, stub tint,
                         formatting per column, a grey-budget rule
6. TITLES & ANNOTATIONS  title + subtitle (both required), caption and source
                         when known, stacked footer notes
7. RENDER & VERIFY       save the table, read it back, audit every rule
```

The order is fixed on purpose. Color intent (step 3) is decided before the quiet
polish (step 5), and the heading band (step 4) can only be decided once the color
decision is already made.

Step 7 is not a vibe check, either. The most recent revision turned "read it back and
audit every rule" into an explicit eight-item checklist: title and subtitle both set,
a real frame, visible hairlines, two separate footer notes instead of one, the
striping gate counted rather than guessed, stub tint checked independently of
striping, every hero measure the request names either colored or bold, and no more
than two colored measures total, recounted by hand. An item you never evaluated the
gate for is not "not applicable" — the checklist makes you compute the condition and
check it for real, every time.

### What actually happens when the model runs it

The skill is not a suggestion the model glances at once. It is a chain of files the
model is routed through, one hop at a time, before it is allowed to write a line of
table code. Here is what that looked like on a real run, prompted with "Show me a
table of the gt cars with their horsepower and price":

```
Skill({"skill": "great-tables"})
Read   references/REFERENCE.md              the router, read first, as instructed
Read   gtcars.csv                            then the data
Read   (4 reads into references/)            data-cleaning + Big-Color rules for
                                              these two numeric measures specifically
Read   references/big_color/column_label_emphasis.md   the heading-band decision
Write  table.py
```

The model's own commentary tracked the routing exactly: "Let me start by reading the
REFERENCE.md file as instructed by the skill," then, once it reached the data, "Since
we have two numeric measures (horsepower and price), I need to read the relevant
references." Nothing in that sequence is the model deciding "I like blue" in the
moment. Every file it opened was named by the router because of what the request and
the data looked like, not because it seemed like a good idea at the time.

### Does it actually work?

Take a different prompt from the same evaluation corpus, one that names a real
structural requirement instead of just a topic: *"Build a table showing the top 10
most expensive gt cars, grouped by country of origin, including their drivetrain and
transmission details."* Ten cars, three countries, a price column, and an explicit
grouping instruction — a good test of what a model does when the request names a
requirement, not just a subject.

**Before**, no skill loaded, the model doing whatever seemed reasonable in the moment:

![](gtcars_baseline.png){width="82%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="A plain table of the ten most expensive GT cars with no color, no row grouping, and Country repeated as an ordinary text column."}

<p style="font-size: 12px;">The baseline run: Country repeated as a plain text column
instead of a real row group, Manufacturer and Model kept as two separate columns, no
color anywhere, no frame, and no source note at all.</p>

It runs, and the numbers in it are correct. But scored against the project's own
hand-authored answer key for this prompt, it manages 25 of 90 possible points (27.8
percent): 10 of 51 on Data-compliance, 15 of 39 on Formatting. The prompt's own
"grouped by country of origin" instruction never becomes a real `great_tables` row
group, so the mechanical grouping check fails outright even though a human reader can
still tell what the table is going for. There is no stub, no color, no frame, no
hairlines between rows, and one title/subtitle with nothing in the footer.

**After**, the skill loaded, same prompt, same data:

![](gtcars_skill.png){width="82%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The same ten cars grouped into Italy, United Kingdom, and United States row groups, with the price column colored on a sequential scale and a combined manufacturer-and-model stub."}

<p style="font-size: 12px;">The skill's run: a real row group per country, a stub
combining manufacturer and model, price colored on a sequential scale from lightest up
to the LaFerrari's dark navy high point, humanized Drivetrain and Transmission labels,
a heading band, a frame, and hairlines between rows.</p>

That climbs to 46 of 90 (51.1 percent): 20 of 51 Data-compliance, 26 of 39 Formatting.
The grouping instruction is now a real `groupname_col`, the price column is colored on
a domain-appropriate sequential scale, and the table picked up the frame, hairlines,
and row-group emphasis the checklist requires unconditionally.

**The answer key**, the project's own hand-authored ground truth for this exact
prompt:

![](gtcars_ground_truth.png){width="82%" fig-align="center" fig-alt="The hand-authored ground truth table: a bare Model stub, MSRP colored sequentially, and a two-line footer with an analytical caption and a separate source note."}

<p style="font-size: 12px;">The answer key: a bare "Model" stub with no manufacturer
prefix, the country groups reordered so United States sits between Italy and United
Kingdom, and two separate footer notes — one stating how "most expensive" and the sort
order were defined, the other citing the source data.</p>

The gap between the skill's table and the answer key is worth naming as honestly as
the gap it already closed. The skill's table still calls `tab_source_note` only once,
a single combined line, not the two the newest checklist item specifically added to
catch this. It still skips row striping on a ten-row body that is not fully covered by
color, the exact gate the project's evaluation corpus keeps catching runs of this skill
missing. Its stub reads "Ferrari LaFerrari," manufacturer folded into the model name,
where the answer key's row identity is the bare model alone, "LaFerrari" — a naming
mismatch, not a wrong car. And its group order is Italy, United Kingdom, United States,
alphabetical among the two "United" names, while the answer key reorders to Italy,
United States, United Kingdom specifically so the group sequence itself still reads
most-expensive-first — the US's single $447,000 entry outranks every UK car, so it
has to come before the UK group for that to hold across the whole table, not just
inside each one.

### Does this hold up past one prompt?

One prompt is an anecdote. The project's own evaluation corpus runs six prompts
spanning easy, medium, and hard difficulty and different data shapes: car listings,
monthly air-quality summaries, town population growth, island populations, and
monthly S&P 500 returns. Each prompt runs three repeats with the skill plus one
baseline run with no skill, every run scored against its own hand-authored answer key
the same way as above — against a comparator that has itself been tightened since the
first version of this post. Two consensus-tuning passes removed six checks that scored
near-zero or scored identically for every skill regardless of quality, so what is left
actually discriminates real differences instead of penalizing every run alike for
something none of them do.

![](comparator_score.png)

<p style="font-size: 12px;">Comparator score across all three repeats and the
baseline run, for each of the six corpus prompts. The skill's repeats cluster well
above the baseline on every single prompt.</p>

Averaged across all six prompts, the skill scores 74.9 percent against a 25.7 percent
baseline — nearly three times over. One honest asterisk on that baseline number: one of
the six baseline runs failed for a harness reason rather than a design one, a
variable-naming mismatch that cost it credit for what was otherwise a normal render;
leaving it out, the baseline reads closer to 28 percent, still a wide gap. The skill's
own side of the comparison is also the most repeatable outcome measured on this
corpus: a mean spread of only 10.6 points between the best and worst of three repeats
on the same prompt, the tightest spread measured yet for this skill.

![](consistency.png)

<p style="font-size: 12px;">Minimum, mean, and maximum comparator score across three
repeats per prompt, skill against baseline. A single baseline run has no spread to
show, since it is only run once per prompt.</p>

None of this is free, and we are not rounding that part away either. The skill's
extra reference reads show up directly in cost: a mean of $0.167 per invocation
against the baseline's $0.077, more than double, for the reads that happen before a
single line of table code gets written. Token use moves the same direction for the
same reason.

![](cost.png)

<p style="font-size: 12px;">Cost per invocation, skill against baseline, by
prompt.</p>

![](tokens.png)

<p style="font-size: 12px;">Total tokens per invocation (input, output, and cache
creation), skill against baseline, by prompt.</p>

### How we made it good

The flowchart itself traces back to a concrete problem, not a hunch: two early
reference tables built for this project, a car-sales ranking and a town-growth
summary, looked like they came from two different products. Every rule since then,
the two-measure ceiling on color, the rule that a light band only appears alongside
Big Color, the grey-budget rule that promotes one neutral surface to a tint when too
many grey elements stack up, traces back to making tables from two different domains
still read as one.

Writing down where the values lived was not enough by itself. A forensic read of
early runs showed the model never opening a single reference file that held
a pinned value, across a dozen repeats. So the skill's instructions went through two
rewrites, not just a wording pass: the first cut the top-level instructions from 976
lines to 225 by extracting a long API reference into its own file; a second pass went
further and restructured everything around a single doorway, one router file that
names every other filename, with the top-level instructions themselves cut down to
117 lines that name decisions but hold no values of their own. A later audit of over
a hundred and fifty real run transcripts found defects a design review alone would not
have caught: none of six flagship examples complied with the skill's own frame rule,
and a summary row once rendered as raw floating-point noise because currency
formatting does not reach grand summary rows by default. Each became a named,
specific fix rather than a general rewrite.

A newer audit went further still, and looked specifically at what was still going
wrong rather than rewriting broadly again. It surfaced two gaps that never fail
outright, they just quietly under-deliver. Given two numeric measures with no explicit
ranking between them — "horsepower and price," for instance — the flowchart's own "at
most two colored measures" ceiling was being read as permission to color both, when
the checklist actually wants one hero measure colored and the other bold instead. And
the footer rule was being satisfied by a single source line that named where the data
came from without ever stating what the table's own numbers meant — technically
present, never analytical. Both are now named, gated rules instead of left to
judgment: a hero-measure tie-break that picks exactly one colored measure when two are
named with no ranking, and an explicit two-call footer requirement that a single
combined source-and-caption line no longer satisfies.

### Where it still falls short

The striping miss above was not only this one candidate's problem. A separate,
independent run of the skill against this same prompt missed the identical gate — a
body with at least ten rows that is not fully covered by color, still missing
`opt_row_striping()` — even though the other repeats of that same run got it right.
Right most of the time, wrong often enough that it is not a typo: that is exactly why
the checklist now spells the gate out as something to count, not eyeball. We are
naming it here rather than picking a cleaner example to show instead.

There is also a structural limit worth stating plainly: inside this project's own
evaluation harness, the routing works because the skill is the only thing loaded and
the harness controls what the agent can reach. Once a skill is published for general
use, nothing stops an agent from skipping the mandated reads and writing table code
straight from memory. The flowchart is a strong default, not an enforced constraint,
outside the environment that was built to test it.

### Try it

The skill lives at `skills/great-tables/` in this repository, and installs the same
way any other skill on this site does, point an agent's skill installer at it, or
copy the folder into your own project. Reading `references/REFERENCE.md` first is the
one rule that matters most; it is the single place every other filename in the skill
lives, and it is written to be read before any data or any Python.

We are glad to talk more about any of this, the flowchart, the comparator, or where
either one should go next, over on our [Discord server](https://discord.com/invite/Ux7nrcXHVV).
